title: The Stuff You Should Know Doin’ Science Playlist: Elastics: Where God and Science Smooch
summary: Rerun of the 2017 Stuff You Should Know episode on elastics, presented as part of the "Doin' Science" playlist. Hosts trace elastic from early loincloths and breeches through the invention of union suits, the ACE bandage, and the looms that weave elastic. They cover the history of rubber from indigenous Amazon use and European exploration, Charles Goodyear's vulcanization and the Hancock/Macintosh rivalry, the rubber band, World War II synthetic rubber, DuPont's Lycra/spandex, the chemistry of elastomers and glass transition temperature, and how rubber degrades. The episode ends with a Pat Benatar spandex anecdote and listener mail about Charlie Chaplin's body-snatching film, a note on the D.B. Cooper tie evidence, and a non-binary listener's pronoun correction.

segments.title: Playlist intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Doin' Science playlist episode on elastics, and the hosts banter about being sick and the idea of dinner party factoids.

segments.title: What elastic is and early undergarments
segments.summary: Elastic is defined as rubber or synthetic thread woven with another fabric such as cotton or nylon. The hosts discuss how elastic waistbands are a recent invention, and the history of loincloths, breechcloths, and breeches.

segments.title: Union suits and long johns
segments.summary: The union suit is described as a one-piece garment, invented in response to the corset craze and the footbinding-like deformation of women's waists. Its access hatch is also covered.

segments.title: ACE bandage and weaving on looms
segments.summary: The ACE bandage, introduced by 3M in 1918, is described as an all-cotton elastic bandage. The hosts note it took until the 1940s for elastic to be applied to underpants. They then discuss how looms interlace warp and weft threads to make elastic fabric.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break in the middle of the episode.

segments.title: Where elastic appears in clothing
segments.summary: The hosts list everyday garments containing elastic, such as socks, shirt necks, shoe tongues, and pleated jeans with elastic waistbands.

segments.title: Pirates, rubber discovery, and Goodyear's vulcanization
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a historian's view of pirates, then explorers finding rubber in Central and South America from indigenous peoples. Rubber fell apart in cold temperatures. Joseph Priestley named rubber by erasing pencil marks. Charles Goodyear's vulcanization with sulfur is contrasted with Thomas Hancock's reverse engineering and patent, and the Goodyear company is named in his honor.

segments.title: Shark Tank tangent and Steve Miller
segments.summary: The hosts digress on the TV show Shark Tank, business equity decisions, and Steve Miller's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction remarks.

segments.title: Rubber trade, Brazil, Malaysia, and rubber band invention
segments.summary: Brazil became a major power through rubber during the Industrial Revolution. British businessmen moved rubber trees to Southeast Asia in the 1870s, shifting the global market. The hosts then note World War II demand, and the invention of the rubber band by Stephen Perry and Thomas Barnabas Daft, and how rubber bands are made today.

segments.title: Synthetic rubber and spandex
segments.summary: Synthetic rubber was developed during and after World War II, and DuPont later created spandex, with the trade name Lycra, by forcing polyurethane polymer through small holes. Spandex accepts dye, is washable, and snaps back, and is in many American clothing items.

segments.title: Chemistry of elastomers and rubber degradation
segments.summary: Elastomers are polymers made of long chains of monomers that straighten under force and coil back on release. Glass transition temperature explains why rubber is flexible at normal temperatures and becomes brittle in cold. Vulcanization links polymer chains with sulfur, and ozone, UV light, and cold cause rubber to degrade over time.

segments.title: Pat Benatar and the eighties spandex trend
segments.summary: The hosts recount that Pat Benatar began the eighties spandex rocker trend after wearing a Catwoman of the Moon-style spandex outfit at Catch a Rising Star on Halloween 1977, which drew a strong crowd response.

segments.title: Listener mail and D.B. Cooper tie evidence
segments.summary: A listener from Pittsburgh writes about Charlie Chaplin's body-snatching film partner's name and the Yiddish-related word ganef. The hosts discuss new evidence about D.B. Cooper's tie linked to Boeing. The listener, BD, then emails a pronoun correction, and the hosts acknowledge it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and contact information and sign off.
